chapters.title: Chapter 5: Putting Sector Rotation Into Practice

lessons.title: Core and Satellite: How Much of Your Portfolio Should Chase the Cycle

body.text: Sector rotation should change the edges of a portfolio, not its foundation. The size of your tactical bets decides whether a wrong call costs you a bad year or a lost decade.

children.text: You now have a way to read the cycle, a set of sector hypotheses, and a view on which vehicle to use. The question left is the one most investors get wrong: how much of the portfolio should act on any of this? This lesson gives you a structure, the arithmetic of position sizing, and rules to keep a rotation strategy from quietly becoming a concentrated gamble.
The Core and Satellite Structure

markDefs.definition: A portfolio split into a large, diversified core meant to capture long-run market returns cheaply, and a smaller set of satellite positions used to express active views such as sector tilts.

children.text: The standard answer is a
core and satellite portfolio

. The core is broad and boring: diversified index funds or diversified active funds you hold through the cycle. Satellites are the sector and theme tilts that come from your cycle work. Commonly quoted ranges put the core at 70% to 90% of the portfolio and satellites at 10% to 30%.

cells: Capture long-run market returns for your goals
Add return from specific sector or theme views
10% to 30%, split across a few tilts
Diversified index funds or diversified active funds
Sector index funds, sector ETFs, thematic funds, or a few stocks
Years to decades, through the cycle
Months to a few years, while the thesis holds
Rebalance on a schedule; rarely changed
Reviewed against the scorecard and relative strength
The loss is capped by the size you chose

children.text: The Arithmetic of Position Size
Before setting a size, be honest about what a tilt can actually contribute. A satellite position changes your portfolio return by its weight multiplied by how much it beats or lags the market.

body.caption: w = the weight of the sector tilt; the bracket is the sector's outperformance in percentage points

children.text: Use real numbers. In 2026 up to 15 September, Nifty IT returned -22.0% against the Nifty 50's -11.5%, so it lagged by about 10.5 percentage points. Nifty Pharma beat the market by about 26.8 percentage points.

body.caption: What a tilt actually adds or costs (2026 to 15 September, price returns)

body.title: Size the Impact
body.prompt: You put 10% of your portfolio into a Nifty IT index fund and the rest in a Nifty 50 index fund. In 2026 to 15 September, Nifty IT returned -22.0% and the Nifty 50 returned -11.5%. By how many percentage points did the tilt change your portfolio return? Give the answer to two decimal places, with a minus sign if it reduced returns.
body.explanation: The tilt lagged by -10.5 pp, and 10% of that is -1.05 pp. Notice how modest the effect is. A 10% tilt that goes badly wrong costs about one percentage point of portfolio return; the same 10% tilt in pharma would have added about 2.68 pp. Small satellites limit damage, but they also limit the reward, which is exactly the trade-off you are choosing.

body.text: This arithmetic cuts both ways, and it is the most useful discipline in the whole course. If a 10% tilt can only move your portfolio by about a percentage point, it is not worth losing sleep over, or worth paying high costs and short-term taxes to chase. If you want a sector call to matter, it has to be large, and then a wrong call really hurts. Choose deliberately.

children.text: What a Single Sector Can Do to You

Sector indices fall much further than the market. The chart below shows the worst peak-to-trough fall on month-end closing values for each index between January 2024 and 15 September 2026, a period with no crisis on the scale of 2008 or 2020.

body.title: Worst peak-to-trough fall on month-end closes, January 2024 to 15 September 2026 (%)

children.text: The Nifty 50 fell 14.8% at worst. Nifty Realty fell 41.1% and Nifty IT 39.3%, the latter sliding from December 2024 all the way to June 2026, about eighteen months. Defence, energy, and FMCG each fell more than 30%. Any of these could have been a conviction satellite position at the start of the period.

body.text: These are index-level falls. Individual stocks within a sector fall further, and month-end data understates intra-month lows. Size every sector position by asking what happens to your plan if it falls 40% and stays there for two years, not by how confident you feel today.

children.text: Setting Your Satellite Budget

cells: Investors near a goal, or new to sector investing
Experienced investors with a long horizon and a written process
Investors who accept large tracking risk and monitor closely

children.text: Cap each sector, not just the total. Three tilts of 10% in banks, PSU banks, and financial services is a 30% bet on one thing.
Count what you already own. If your diversified core is a Nifty 50 index fund, you already hold over 36% financial services, so a financials tilt adds to an existing overweight.
Keep money for near-term goals out of satellites entirely. Tilts belong to money with years of runway, after an emergency fund is in place.
Limit the number of tilts. Two or three sector positions you can actually monitor beat six you cannot.
Rules That Keep a Satellite a Satellite
Without rules, satellites drift. Winners grow into dangerous positions, and losers get held with new justifications. Two mechanisms solve most of this.
1. Rebalancing Bands

Set a target weight and a band around it. With a 10% target and a 25% relative band, you act only when the position drifts outside 7.5% to 12.5% of the portfolio. Bands avoid constant tinkering while preventing a winning tilt from quietly doubling.

body.title: Find the Trigger
body.prompt: Your target satellite weight for one sector is 10% of the portfolio, and you use a 25% relative rebalancing band. At what portfolio weight does the position trigger a trim? Give the answer as a percentage to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 10% x 1.25 = 12.5%, and the lower trigger is 10% x 0.75 = 7.5%. Between those levels you do nothing. Trimming back to target after a strong run is what turns a good sector call into a realised gain instead of an unplanned concentration, though remember from Lesson 5.1 that trimming within 12 months means short-term capital gains tax at 20%.

children.text: 2. A Written Thesis and Exit Test

Every satellite should have a one-line thesis drawn from your scorecard and relative strength work, plus the conditions that would end it. Thesis-based exits are better than price-based ones for cycle tilts, because a sector can fall while the thesis is intact, and can rise while it quietly breaks.

columns.label: Rules-based
points: Target weight and band written down before buying
Thesis stated in one line, with named exit conditions
Scheduled review, for example quarterly, with the scorecard
Tax and cost checked before switching
Position size set by what a 40% fall would do to the plan

columns.label: Feel-based
points: Position size decided by conviction on the day
Thesis changes to fit whatever the price is doing
Reviewed when the sector is in the news
Switches made on impulse, costs noticed later
Size justified by how sure you feel

body.title: Go deeper: why satellites are riskier than their weight suggests

children.text: Weight is not the same as risk. A sector index that is far more volatile than the market contributes more risk than its weight implies. Lesson 3.4 showed Nifty Pharma and Nifty FMCG with betas around 0.6 while Nifty IT was near 1.0, and the drawdown chart above shows realty and IT falling roughly two to three times as far as the Nifty 50.
A position in a sector that is twice as volatile as the market carries roughly double the risk of the same weight in the market itself.
That is why a 10% cap on a high-beta sector such as realty or metals is not unduly cautious, while the same cap on a defensive sector is genuinely conservative.
A simple adjustment is to scale a position down in proportion to how much more volatile the sector has been than the index.
Check volatility and beta on the index factsheet before sizing, not after the position has moved.
Practice

body.title: Name the Structure
body.textWithBlank: A portfolio built as a large diversified base plus smaller tactical sector tilts is called a ___ and satellite portfolio.
body.explanation: The core, typically 70% to 90%, carries your long-term goals. Satellites, typically 10% to 30%, carry your active sector views, sized so that being wrong is survivable.

body.title: Spot the Hidden Concentration
body.question: Your core is a Nifty 50 index fund. You then add 10% each in a banking fund, a PSU bank fund, and a financial services fund as separate satellites. What is the main problem?
options: Nothing: three different funds means three different bets
The three satellites are largely the same bet on financials, and your Nifty 50 core already has over 36% in financial services
Satellites should always be equal weighted
Sector funds cannot be combined with index funds
body.explanation: All three satellites express one view: that financials will outperform. Added to a core with over 36% financial services weight, the portfolio becomes a concentrated bet on a single part of the economy. Cap exposure by sector group, not by fund count, and count your core exposure before adding a tilt.

cards.definition: The diversified, long-held majority of the portfolio, typically 70% to 90%, meant to deliver market returns cheaply.
A smaller tactical position, typically part of a 10% to 30% allocation, used to express a sector or theme view.
A range around a target weight, such as 25% relative, outside which you trim or top up the position.
The worst peak-to-trough fall over a period. Nifty Realty's was about 41% between January 2024 and September 2026.
The risk that your portfolio behaves very differently from the market because of active tilts.
Selling because the reason for owning a sector has changed, rather than because the price moved.

body.title: Fix the Portfolio
body.scenario: Rahul, 34, invests ₹60,000 a month for retirement, decades away. Over two years he has added sector positions as they appeared in the news: defence 15%, PSU banks 12%, railways PSU 8%, and an IT fund 10%, which is 45% of his equity portfolio in four tilts. The rest sits in a Nifty 50 index fund. His railways and IT positions are deep in the red, and he has no written thesis for any of them. He is considering adding a metals fund because it has performed well recently.
body.prompt: What are the main problems with this portfolio, and what would a disciplined core and satellite structure look like for him?
body.modelAnswer: Three problems stand out. First, size: 45% in four sector tilts is not a satellite allocation, it is the portfolio. His outcome now depends mainly on sector calls rather than on market returns. Second, correlation: defence, PSU banks, and railways PSUs are largely one bet on government capex and public sector re-rating, so the true concentration is worse than the split suggests. Third, process: with no written thesis, he cannot tell whether the railways and IT losses reflect a broken thesis or normal volatility, and buying metals because it has recently performed well is chasing, the late signal from Lesson 4.2. A disciplined structure for a 34-year-old with a long horizon might be a core of 80% in diversified index funds, with satellites capped at 20% in total and no more than 10% in any one sector group, counting defence, PSU banks, and railways as a single group. Each remaining tilt gets a one-line thesis from his scorecard, a target weight, a rebalancing band, and named exit conditions. Because unwinding will trigger capital gains, he should plan the sequence with holding periods and taxes in mind, as Lesson 5.1 describes, and consider directing new monthly investments into the core rather than selling everything at once.

body.label: NSE Indices: Factsheets with Volatility and Beta
body.description: Index factsheets showing standard deviation, beta, and returns, useful for sizing a sector position by risk rather than by conviction.

body.text: This lesson is educational and the allocation templates are illustrative, not personalised advice. Drawdown and return figures are calculated from NSE month-end closing values, exclude dividends, and describe the past. Your own allocation depends on your goals, horizon, and risk capacity; consider consulting a SEBI registered investment adviser.

points: Sector rotation belongs in satellites, typically 10% to 30% of the portfolio, around a diversified core of 70% to 90%
Portfolio impact equals weight times outperformance: a 10% IT tilt in 2026 to mid September changed returns by about -1.05 pp, and a 10% pharma tilt by about 2.68 pp
Small tilts cannot transform returns; large tilts can wreck them. Choose the trade-off deliberately
Sector drawdowns dwarf the market: between January 2024 and September 2026 the Nifty 50 fell 14.8% at worst, while realty fell about 41% and IT about 39% over roughly eighteen months
Cap exposure by sector group, and count the sector weight already inside your core before adding a tilt
Use rebalancing bands: a 10% target with a 25% relative band means acting only outside 7.5% to 12.5%
Write a one-line thesis and exit conditions for every satellite, and review on a schedule rather than when the sector is in the news
